title: Thinking About Coverage Needs
summary: Start by mapping where the business could injure someone, damage property, use vehicles, employ staff, store tools, or sign contracts that require certificates.
considerations: Client-site service work often raises general liability and property damage questions.
Vehicles used for jobs may need separate commercial auto review.
Employees can trigger workers compensation obligations that vary by jurisdiction.
Tools and mobile equipment may need scheduling or inland-marine-style coverage review.

title: Claim Readiness Basics
summary: A software workflow can help collect facts consistently, but real claim decisions belong to the insurer or authorized claims professional.
considerations: Record the date, location, people involved, photos, and immediate safety steps.
Keep damaged property, receipts, and contracts when safe and practical.
Avoid admitting fault in a software note; document facts neutrally.
Contact the actual carrier or licensed representative for claim filing instructions.

title: Certificate Workflow Planning
summary: A demo can show how a business tracks certificate requests, but real certificates must be issued through authorized insurance channels.
considerations: Capture the requesting party, job location, project dates, and required wording.
Flag requests for additional insured or waiver wording for review.
Compare certificate requirements against current policy limits before accepting a job.
Store request history so renewals and recurring clients are easier to manage.

title: Quote Comparison Framing
summary: A clean comparison should separate price from coverage fit, missing lines, deductibles, and operational assumptions.
considerations: Cheapest is not automatically best if key exposures are missing.
A package can fit one trade but be a poor fit for another.
Synthetic scoring is useful for demos, not for underwriting or advice.
Real quotes depend on applications, state rules, carrier appetite, and underwriting review.
